Baby & Child

2 Month Old Milestones: What Babies Do by 2 Months

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

By 2 months, most babies smile when you talk to them, calm down when picked up, coo, react to loud sounds, watch you as you move, look at faces, hold their head up during tummy time, and move both arms and both legs. These skills come from the CDC's revised checklist, which describes what most babies, about 75 percent, can already do by this age. This guide walks through each area, adds a feeding and sleep snapshot, and covers exactly when to call your baby's clinician.

What a 2 month milestone checklist really means

In 2022, the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics revised their milestone checklists so each item describes what most babies, around 75 percent, can already do by that age. Before the change, many items described the average age, which meant half of all healthy babies had not reached them yet. The new framing makes the list easier to use: if your baby shows a skill, that is reassuring, and if a skill is missing at 2 months, it is a clear signal to mention at the checkup rather than a reason to panic. The checklist ages line up with well visits on purpose, so the 2 month visit is the natural moment to review it.

Normal still covers a wide range. Babies work on skills unevenly, so yours might coo constantly but protest tummy time, or follow a slowly moving toy with their eyes while barely smiling yet. If your baby was born early, count from the due date rather than the birth date, so a baby born six weeks early is compared with the 2 week mark, not the 2 month mark. The most useful habit is simple: watch for these skills over a couple of weeks in calm, alert moments, note what you see, and bring the notes to the visit. Comparing your baby with a sibling or another baby the same age tells you very little.

Social smiles, cooing, and hearing

The social changes are the ones most parents feel first. By 2 months, most babies calm down when spoken to or picked up, look at your face, seem pleased when you come close, and smile when you talk to or smile at them. That first social smile often appears somewhere around 6 to 8 weeks, and it is different from the fleeting smiles of a sleeping newborn: it happens while your baby is awake, looking at you, and responding to you. If your baby has not smiled yet at the visit, say so. Some babies simply need a little longer, and the clinician will want to check hearing and vision as part of the picture.

Language at this age means sounds and reactions, not words. Listen for cooing, those soft vowel sounds like ooh and aah, and notice whether your baby reacts to loud sounds by startling, blinking, going quiet, or crying. You can build both skills in ordinary moments. Hold your baby about 8 to 12 inches from your face, talk slowly during feeds and diaper changes, then pause and wait. Many babies will answer with a sound or a wriggle, and that pause teaches the rhythm of conversation. There is no need for special toys or apps. Your voice and your face are the most interesting things your baby has ever encountered.

Head control, tracking, and movement

On the movement side, most 2 month olds can hold their head up when lying on their tummy, move both arms and both legs, and briefly open their hands. Head control is still wobbly, so keep supporting the head when you lift and carry your baby. During tummy time, expect short lifts of the head rather than a steady push-up, and keep every session supervised while your baby is awake; our newborn tummy time guide covers how to build from there. Pay attention to symmetry too. Babies should use both sides of the body, so mention it at the visit if one arm or leg seems to move much less than the other.

Thinking skills at 2 months show up as attention. Most babies this age watch you as you move around the room and can look at a toy or face for several seconds. Vision is still developing, so high contrast helps: bold black and white patterns, a slowly moving rattle, or simply your face drifting from one side to the other. Try moving an object slowly across your baby's field of view and watch the eyes follow it. Brief eye crossing can still be normal this early, but eyes that seem constantly crossed or never track anything are worth mentioning to the clinician. Short, repeated moments of this kind of play do more than long sessions.

Feeding and sleep at 2 months

Feeding is still frequent at this age. Breastfed babies typically nurse 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, though the pattern often becomes a little more predictable than in the newborn weeks. Formula fed babies usually take larger feeds less often, commonly every 3 to 4 hours. Rather than watching the clock, watch your baby: steady weight gain, plenty of wet diapers, and a baby who seems settled after most feeds are the reassuring signs. Growth spurts can temporarily turn everything upside down, with a day or two of near constant feeding, and then things settle again. If feeding hurts, takes a very long time at every session, or your baby rarely seems satisfied, raise it at the checkup.

Most 2 month olds sleep roughly 14 to 17 hours across a full day and night, usually in short, irregular stretches. Some babies begin to give one longer stretch at night around now, and many do not; both patterns are common. Day and night confusion usually eases as you keep days bright and interactive and nights dark, quiet, and boring. Keep following safe sleep basics at every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, in the parents' room but in the baby's own crib or bassinet, with no loose blankets, pillows, or soft toys. A short, repeatable wind down, such as a feed, a fresh diaper, and a song, helps more than any gadget.

The 2 month checkup and when to call

The 2 month well visit usually includes weight, length, and head measurements, a full physical exam, and a conversation about feeding, sleep, and the milestones above. This is also the visit where the first big round of routine immunizations happens, so plan a quieter day afterward; mild fussiness or a sleepy afternoon is common. Come with questions written down, because they evaporate the moment you are in the room. It helps to note dates, feeding patterns, and anything you have wondered about in the BeMama app or a notebook during the weeks before, then skim your notes in the waiting room. No question about your own baby is too small for this visit.

A few signs deserve a conversation sooner rather than later. Talk with your baby's clinician if, by 2 months, your baby does not respond to loud sounds, does not watch things as they move, does not smile at people, does not bring hands toward the mouth, or cannot hold the head up at all when pushing up during tummy time. At any age, losing a skill a baby once had deserves prompt attention. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis, and checklists cannot examine your baby. If something feels off to you, even something you cannot name, say it out loud at the visit. Early questions lead to early answers, and most of those answers are reassuring.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC milestones describe skills that most children can do by a particular age across social, language, thinking, and movement domains. They support observation and conversation but do not replace standardized developmental screening.

Individual skills vary, but caregiver concern matters. Missing several expected skills, losing a skill, or a difference in movement, communication, hearing, or vision should be discussed promptly.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to preserve dated observations, growth, activities, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot label development as normal or delayed.

When to seek help

Contact your child’s healthcare professional whenever you are concerned or notice loss of a skill. Seek urgent care for an acute change, breathing difficulty, loss of responsiveness, or seizure-like activity.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Milestone checklists describe what most babies do by 2 months, so a missing skill is a conversation starter, not a verdict.
  • Look for social smiles, cooing, calming when picked up, and clear reactions to loud sounds.
  • Most 2 month olds hold their head up briefly in tummy time and move both arms and both legs.
  • Expect 8 to 12 feeds a day for breastfed babies and roughly 14 to 17 hours of sleep in short stretches.
  • Call the clinician about lost skills, no response to loud sounds, no visual tracking, or no smiles at people.

Frequently asked questions

What should a 2 month old be doing?

By 2 months, most babies smile at people, coo, calm down when picked up or spoken to, react to loud sounds, watch moving things and faces, hold their head up briefly during tummy time, and move both arms and both legs. These items describe what most babies can do by this age, not a strict deadline. If several are missing, or anything worries you, bring the checklist to your baby's clinician.

When do babies start smiling?

Most babies give their first social smile somewhere around 6 to 8 weeks, and by 2 months most smile when you talk to or smile at them. Earlier fleeting smiles during sleep are reflexive rather than social. If your baby is not smiling at people by the 2 month visit, mention it; some babies need a little longer, and the clinician can check hearing and vision.

How much should a 2 month old sleep?

Most 2 month olds sleep roughly 14 to 17 hours in a 24 hour period, usually in short, irregular stretches around the clock. Some begin one longer nighttime stretch around now, and many do not. Keep days bright and nights dark and quiet, and follow safe sleep guidance at every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, with nothing loose in the sleep space.

When should I worry about my 2 month old?

Contact your baby's clinician if your 2 month old does not respond to loud sounds, does not watch things as they move, does not smile at people, cannot hold the head up during tummy time, or has lost a skill they once had. A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher needs medical attention right away at this age. Feeding refusal, few wet diapers, or unusual floppiness or stiffness also deserve a prompt call. Trust your instincts; asking early is never a mistake.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
